newsitem.title: ITALY: Friedman says EMU will have trouble working.
newsitem.headline: Friedman says EMU will have trouble working.

text.p: European countries will have trouble making a currency union work because their economies are not flexible enough to cope with unexpected shocks, U.S. Nobel prize-winning economist Milton Friedman said in an interview.
Friedman told news weekly Panorama that the planned single currency, the euro, was "a bad idea."

Friedman, who won the Nobel prize for economics in 1976, popularised free-market and monetarist ideas which influenced U.S. President Ronald Reagan and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s.

For a currency union to work "you need countries which are relatively homogeneous in their economic structure and able to respond in the same way to any shocks, those chance effects which influence an economy," said Friedman.
"The various countries which are getting ready to enter the the euro do not have these characteristics in common," he added.
He said it would be better for political union to take shape before a monetary union went ahead.
"In Europe countries are politically independent and each one speaks a different language. There is no single labour market and there is limited mobility between one country and another," he said.
European countries would find it much easier to create a single market and abolish trade barriers with flexible exchange rates rather than in a currency union.
He said if Italy were part of a currency union it would be in difficulty if an external shock were to hit it harder than other countries in the region.

"How could Italy react? With the euro the only way is deflation, that is lowering prices and favouring a depression. With flexible exchange rates it can react in such a way as to obtain a realignment," he added.

Friedman described the criteria for EMU membership laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, which Italy is trying hard to fulfil, as "simple obstacles ... to restrict the number of countries which can join."
